q: A 3-year-old girl has had a swollen right knee for 2 months. She is well; ANA is positive. The most important screening for her is:
e: ANA-positive oligoarticular JIA carries a high risk of silent chronic anterior uveitis.

q: The minimum duration of arthritis required to diagnose JIA is:
e: JIA: onset before 16 years, arthritis ≥ 6 weeks, other causes excluded.

q: The commonest subtype of JIA is:
e: Oligoarticular JIA accounts for about half of cases.

q: A 4-year-old has had daily fever spikes for 3 weeks, a salmon-pink rash that appears with the fever, hepatosplenomegaly and swollen knees. Before diagnosing systemic JIA the most important test is:
o: Blood film and bone marrow to exclude leukaemia
e: Leukaemia, kala-azar and TB mimic systemic JIA; steroids may mask leukaemia.

q: All of the following are causes of hepatomegaly EXCEPT:
e: Systemic JIA causes hepatosplenomegaly; physiological jaundice does not cause hepatomegaly.

q: A child with systemic JIA has persistent fever, falling ESR, platelets 60 000/mm³ and ferritin 15 000 ng/mL. The diagnosis is:
e: MAS: fever with falling ESR and blood counts and very high ferritin; treat with IV methylprednisolone.

q: The first-line disease-modifying drug in JIA is:
e: Methotrexate 10–15 mg/m² once weekly with folic acid.

q: The treatment of choice for a single swollen knee in oligoarticular JIA is:
e: Intra-articular steroid injection is the treatment of choice in oligoarticular disease.

q: A boy of 12 years with heel pain, low back stiffness and a painful red eye most likely has JIA associated with:
e: Enthesitis-related arthritis: older boys, HLA-B27, acute anterior uveitis.

q: A child with JIA of the left knee has a longer left leg. This is due to:
o: Overgrowth from inflammation near the growth plate
e: Inflammation increases blood flow to the growth plate, giving leg-length discrepancy.
